opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been thinking about a lot, because the default assumption in the field has been pretty simple: more pre-training data, more compute, lower pre-training loss, and that should translate into a better model for whatever you want to do downstream. And for a long time that was largely true, so it became a kind of article of faith.

But what we've been finding is that the relationship is more subtle than that. Specifically, if you take a model and pre-train it for longer and longer, past a certain point it can actually become *harder* to fine-tune. We've been calling this something like catastrophic overtraining. The base model looks better by the usual metrics, its pre-training loss keeps going down, but when you then fine-tune it, whether that's instruction tuning or adapting it to some specific domain, the final model can end up worse than one that started from a checkpoint with less pre-training.

The way I think about why this happens is in terms of sensitivity. As you keep pre-training, the parameters become progressively more sensitive to perturbation. Fine-tuning is essentially a perturbation: you're moving the weights to adapt to a new task. If the model has become very brittle, those updates end up disrupting a lot of what it learned in pre-training. So you get more forgetting, and the knowledge you paid so much compute to build doesn't carry over the way you'd hope.

So my answer to "does more pre-training make a model better for downstream use?" is: it depends on what you're going to do with it afterward. If you're using the base model as is, then sure, more is often better. But if the model is a starting point for further adaptation, which is how almost everyone uses these models, then you have to think about adaptability as its own property, separate from pre-training loss. And those two things can actually trade off against each other.

I think that has some practical implications. One is that we probably need better ways to evaluate base models, ones that measure how well they hold up after fine-tuning, not just how good they look out of the box. Another is that it opens up interesting research directions, like whether you can change the pre-training recipe, the optimizer, the learning rate schedule, or regularization, to keep the model more plastic while still getting the benefits of scale. It's not that scaling is wrong. It's that "better" is a more multi-dimensional thing than a single loss number captures.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it's much less straightforward than the scaling narrative would suggest. The default assumption in the field has been that more pre-training is basically monotonic: you train on more tokens, you get a better base model, and a better base model is a better starting point for whatever you want to do downstream. And for a lot of metrics, like loss on held-out web text or zero-shot performance on standard benchmarks, that's true.

But the thing we got interested in is that "better for downstream use" almost always means "better after you adapt it." Nobody deploys the raw base model. You fine-tune it, you do instruction tuning, you do RLHF, you do some kind of post-training. So the real question is whether a model that's been pre-trained longer is also easier to adapt, and that's where things get interesting, because we found that it's not. There's this phenomenon we've been calling catastrophic overtraining, where if you take checkpoints from the same model at different points in pre-training and fine-tune each one on the same downstream task, the ones that were pre-trained longer can actually end up worse after fine-tuning, even though they started out better.

The intuition we have for why this happens is about sensitivity. As you keep pre-training, the parameters become more sensitive to perturbation. Small changes to the weights produce larger changes in behavior. And fine-tuning is, at the end of the day, a perturbation to the weights. So the same fine-tuning update that was benign on an earlier checkpoint can degrade more of what the model knew on a later checkpoint. You get more forgetting, more drift, and in some regimes that outweighs the gains from the extra pre-training.

So the way I think about it now is that pre-training isn't just building up capabilities, it's also shaping how malleable the model is, and those two things can pull in opposite directions. If your downstream use is purely zero-shot, sure, train longer. But if you're going to adapt it, there's a tradeoff, and the right amount of pre-training depends on how much and how aggressively you're going to modify the model afterward. And I think we don't have a good science of that yet. We have scaling laws for loss, but we don't really have scaling laws for adaptability, and I'd argue that's the quantity that actually matters for most practical uses.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: better after what? If you evaluate a model directly after pre-training, you might see steady improvements as you pre-train longer. But downstream use often involves another step, like fine-tuning on a particular task. And what we really care about is how good the model is after that step.

Those two things don’t necessarily move together. A model can get better during pre-training but become more sensitive to the changes you make during fine-tuning. So you have to look at the combination: how much you pre-train, what downstream data you have, and how you adapt the model.

I wouldn’t treat pre-training performance as a sufficient measure of downstream usefulness. I’d evaluate the whole pipeline, including whether the gains hold up when the downstream distribution differs from the fine-tuning data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is, better in what sense? Typically, we measure progress in pre-training through the loss, and then we look at some downstream benchmarks. But downstream use often involves adapting the model, and it’s not obvious that a model with a better pre-training loss will necessarily be better after that adaptation.

For example, you might care about how much labeled data you need to fine-tune it, or whether it generalizes when the deployment distribution differs from the fine-tuning data. Those are different notions of being better, and they don’t have to move together.

So I would think about the whole pipeline: what the model learns during pre-training, how we adapt it, and what we ultimately evaluate. More pre-training can be very useful, but the question is whether the improvements it produces are improvements that the downstream procedure can actually take advantage of.
